1	# Local Docker Compose stack
2	
3	Implements local sub-issue [02.02 — Define services and shared
4	configuration, including the Control DB and per-project test
5	databases](../../../context/notion-tasks/sub-issues/02-02.md) (parent: [02
6	— Add Docker Compose local stack](../../../context/notion-tasks/02-docker-compose.md)).
7	Builds directly on [the local-stack inventory](local-stack-inventory.md)
8	from the preceding sub-issue — read that document first for the
9	application startup contracts this stack reuses unchanged (it does not
10	re-derive them here).
11	
12	## Scope
13	
14	One Compose file (`docker-compose.yml`, repository root) defines all seven
15	required service responsibilities as real processes/containers:
16	
17	1. `web` — the existing Next.js app, `dev` command.
18	2. `api` — the existing Hono API, `dev` command.
19	3. `worker` — the existing worker **development** process (`tsx watch`) —
20	   not `start`, and not a job processor either way (see "Known
21	   limitations" below).
22	4. `postgres` — one PostgreSQL server, two disposable databases: the
23	   Control DB and a project-test target.
24	5. `nginx` — the reverse proxy; the only published entry point for the
25	   browser.
26	6. `storage` — SeaweedFS, S3-compatible endpoint, single-node mode.
27	7. `mailhog` — local mail capture.
28	
29	Everything here is local-development only. No production target, no TLS,
30	no CI wiring, no business schema, no queue consumer, no storage/mail
31	*application* adapter. `docker-compose.dev.yml` / `docker-compose.test.yml`
32	were not created: `docker-compose.yml` already runs dev-mode processes
33	with live-reload mounts (see "Development mounts" below), so a separate
34	dev overlay was not needed for this sub-issue's scope, and the test
35	harness (`tests/integration/docker-compose/`) achieves isolation via a
36	unique `-p` project name and either a pre-picked free host port
37	(`NGINX_HTTP_PORT` — required because that value is baked into
38	`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` at container start) or an ephemeral host port
39	discovered after startup (`MAILHOG_UI_PORT`/`SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT`, neither
40	read by any application code) instead of a dedicated compose file — see
41	"Tests" below.
42	
43	## Prerequisites
44	
45	- Docker Engine with the Compose V2 CLI plugin (the `docker compose`
46	  subcommand, not the legacy standalone `docker-compose` V1 binary), with
47	  a Linux-container backend. **Verified by real execution** (Docker
48	  Desktop 29.8.2 / `docker compose` plugin v5.5.1, Windows host,
49	  WSL2/Linux-container engine) — see the final report for sub-issue #47
50	  for the exact commands and results. Earlier drafts of this document
51	  were written before Docker was available and said so explicitly; that
52	  caveat no longer applies.
53	- No `pnpm`/Node install needed on the host — every app container installs
54	  its own dependencies at image-build time (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`
55	  against the committed `pnpm-lock.yaml`).
56	- Copy `.env.example` to `.env` at the repository root (same convention as
57	  the existing runtime-config setup — see `README.md` "Runtime
58	  configuration"). Every value in it is a development-only placeholder.
59	- Only for the real-browser check (`tests/e2e/docker-compose/`):
60	  Playwright's Chromium browser binary must be installed
61	  (`pnpm exec playwright install chromium`). **Now installed and
62	  verified** in the environment that ran the sub-issue #47 real
63	  verification (`pnpm run test:e2e` passed with a real Chromium
64	  instance). Installing it remains a deliberate, separately-authorized
65	  step in a fresh checkout — this repository's tooling does not do it on
66	  your own behalf automatically.
67	
68	## Startup
69	
70	```bash
71	docker compose up --build
72	```
73	
74	First run builds `web`, `api`, and `worker`'s images (each installs the
75	full pnpm workspace and bakes an initial `@relis/config` build — see
76	"Clean-checkout startup" below) and provisions two disposable PostgreSQL
77	databases via the `migrate-control` / `migrate-project` one-shot services.
78	Subsequent runs can drop `--build` unless `package.json`/`pnpm-lock.yaml`
79	changed.
80	
81	## Shutdown and reset
82	
83	```bash
84	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml stop                              # stop, keep containers and data
85	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans             # remove containers/network, KEEP data
86	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans   # reset: DELETE this project's data
87	```
88	
89	The last command destroys both local databases and every stored
90	object. Read ["Persistence, lifecycle, and reset"](#persistence-lifecycle-and-reset)
91	below for the full lifecycle table, exactly what a reset deletes, and
92	how to recreate the stack afterward.
93	
94	## Service graph and addresses
95	
96	| Service | Role | Published to host? | Internal address | Notes |
97	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
98	| `nginx` | Reverse proxy | **Yes** — `127.0.0.1:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}` | `nginx:80` | The only entry point for `web`/`api`. |
99	| `web` | Next.js dev | No | `web:3000` | Reached only via `nginx`. |
100	| `api` | Hono dev | No | `api:3001` | Reached only via `nginx`'s `/api/` prefix — never published directly, per this task's "health/readiness only through the proxy" requirement. |
101	| `worker` | Worker dev (`tsx watch`) | n/a (no listener) | n/a | See "Known limitations." |
102	| `postgres` | Control DB + project-test DB | No | `postgres:5432` | Two databases, one server — see "Database isolation." |
103	| `migrate-control` / `migrate-project` | One-shot provisioning | n/a | n/a | Run once at startup, exit 0, do not stay running. |
104	| `storage` | SeaweedFS S3 gateway | **Yes** — `127.0.0.1:${SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT:-8333}` | `storage:8333` | Development-only endpoint; no app adapter consumes it. |
105	| `mailhog` | Mail capture, web UI | **Yes** (UI only) — `127.0.0.1:${MAILHOG_UI_PORT:-8025}` | `mailhog:8025` (UI), `mailhog:1025` (SMTP) | SMTP stays internal — nothing submits mail through it yet. |
106	
107	### Internal vs. host-facing vs. browser-public addresses
108	
109	- **Internal (Compose-only hostnames)**: `postgres:5432`, `api:3001`,
110	  `web:3000`, `storage:8333`/`9333`/`8888`, `mailhog:1025`. These resolve
111	  only inside the Compose network and are never reachable from the host
112	  browser or shell.
113	- **Host-facing (loopback-published)**: `127.0.0.1:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT}`,
114	  `127.0.0.1:${MAILHOG_UI_PORT}`, `127.0.0.1:${SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT}` — reachable
115	  from the host machine (curl, a browser, a local S3 client) but bound to
116	  loopback only, never `0.0.0.0`, per this task's "bind published
117	  development ports to loopback" requirement.
118	- **Browser-public**: `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, set to
119	  `http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}/api` — **not** the internal
120	  `api:3001` hostname. `apps/web/src/app/page.tsx`'s existing client-side
121	  `fetch(`${apiUrl}/health`)` call is unmodified; it now resolves through
122	  nginx's `/api/` prefix (stripped by nginx, reaching `apps/api` as
123	  `GET /health`) instead of a hostname the browser could never resolve.
124	  Because the page itself is also served through the same nginx origin,
125	  this fetch is **same-origin** — no cross-origin request, so the
126	  existing `API_CORS_ORIGIN` setting (still configured, defensively, as
127	  `http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT}`) is not actually exercised in
128	  normal use.
129

139	3. At container start, the `command:` override in `docker-compose.yml`
140	   runs `pnpm --filter @relis/config build` **again** before the real

- `persistence.test.ts` — the real disposable-persistence, scoped-reset,
  and clean-recreation check for both named volumes (see
  ["Persistence, lifecycle, and reset"](#persistence-lifecycle-and-reset)).
  Starts only the two services that own data (`postgres`, `storage`), so
  it builds no application image. In order, against the real daemon:
  - The actual volumes Compose created, confirmed by `docker volume
    inspect`'s own `com.docker.compose.project` / `.volume` labels — an
    ownership record, not a name-prefix guess — and asserted not to be
    `external` and not to have existed beforehand.
  - Every bind mount in the **resolved** configuration is read-only
    configuration or an application source directory; nothing writable
    points at a data directory in the working tree, and neither
    `/var/lib/postgresql/data` nor `/data` is bind-mounted. This is the
    structural reason database/object data cannot become a tracked
    repository artifact.
  - The Control DB and project-test database are distinct at the
    connection targets `migrate-control`/`migrate-project` are actually
    configured with (read from the resolved configuration, with
    credentials discarded — see `resolveComposePersistence`), both exist
    on the one server, and a fixture row planted in each is invisible
    from the other **in both directions**.
  - A fixture row and a real signed-S3-uploaded object survive a
    `stop`/`start`, asserted together with the container ids being
    **unchanged** (so this is genuinely a restart).
  - Both survive `down --remove-orphans` (no `--volumes`) followed by
    `up`, asserted together with the container ids having **changed**
    (genuinely recreated) and both volumes still existing in between.
  - `down --volumes` deletes exactly the recorded volumes; a **second,
    independently-named Compose project** running its own `postgres`
    with its own fixture row is then shown to still have its volume and
    its row. Without that second project, "the reset removed only its
    own volumes" would be vacuous on a daemon with nothing else on it.
  - Recreating afterward works from committed configuration alone, both
    databases are provisioned again by the init path, and the prior
    fixture table and object are **gone**.

  Destructive steps are gated: both project names carry a random suffix,
  volume ownership is confirmed by label immediately before the reset
  (`confirmDisposableOwnershipOrStop` throws rather than deleting on an
  assumption), every volume present before the run is asserted to still
  exist after it, all published ports are ephemeral, and deletion is
  only ever a `-p`-scoped `docker compose down --volumes` — never
  `docker volume rm`, never a prune, never a filesystem deletion. The
  `afterAll` hook tears down **both** projects, reports a failure for
  either without discarding the other, and verifies the result
  (this project's volumes gone, every pre-existing volume still there)
  instead of trusting the exit code.

  the only file here that needs **no Docker daemon** (just `git` and this
  checkout). Read-only Git throughout — `git ls-files`, `git check-ignore
  --no-index`, `git status --porcelain` (helpers in
  `packages/test-utils/src/git.ts`): nothing is ever staged or created to
  probe a rule, and no real secret is written, since `check-ignore
  --no-index` evaluates a path whether or not it exists. Asserts that
  real environment files (root and per-package), generated build output,
  test run output, and the structure-reserved `storage/{uploads,exports,temp}/`
  directories are all ignored; that `.env.example`, the committed
  development configuration (`docker/postgres/init/`,
  `docker/storage/s3-identities.json`, `docker/nginx/nginx.conf`), the
  fixtures, and a `.gitkeep` inside each ignored `storage/` directory all
  stay trackable; that `.env.example` is the only tracked environment
  file and no generated artifact is tracked; that nothing risky is
  sitting untracked in the working tree; and — via `git ls-files -i -c`
  — that **no ignore pattern is broad enough to shadow a tracked source
  file**.

s = io.open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()

old_startup = """# Startup:  docker compose up --build
# Shutdown: docker compose down            (add -v to also drop the
#                                            disposable postgres/storage
#                                            volumes)
"""
new_startup = """# Startup:  docker compose up --build
# Shutdown: docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans
#             -> removes containers/network, KEEPS both named volumes and
#                all local data; `up -d` afterward recreates with data
#                intact.
# Reset:    docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans
#             -> ALSO deletes this project's postgres-data and
#                storage-data volumes. Irreversible: both logical
#                databases and every stored object at once. No backup
#                exists. Never part of ordinary startup, and never a
#                broad `docker ... prune` (that reaches other projects).
# Full lifecycle table, persistence inventory, and clean-recreation
# steps: docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md
#        ("Persistence, lifecycle, and reset").
"""
assert old_startup in s
s = s.replace(old_startup, new_startup, 1)

old_volumes = """volumes:
  postgres-data:
  storage-data:
"""
new_volumes = """# Persistent local data — both DISPOSABLE. Compose prefixes each with the
# project name (`relis_postgres-data` for a default startup from this
# directory), which is what keeps two Compose projects from ever sharing
# one. Deliberately neither `external:` nor explicitly `name:`d: an
# external volume would be a pre-existing resource outside this stack's
# lifecycle, and a fixed name would make every project collide on the
# same data. No host path and no production endpoint is involved.
# See docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md "Persistence, lifecycle,
# and reset" for what each holds and what a reset destroys.
volumes:
  # The whole PostgreSQL cluster: BOTH logical databases (the Control DB
  # and the project-test target) plus server-wide state. One server, one
  # volume, two databases — a volume per database is deliberately NOT a
  # requirement here.
  postgres-data:
  # SeaweedFS's entire single-node state in one directory (master
  # metadata, object/volume files, filer metadata) — i.e. every
  # non-production bucket and object.
  storage-data:
"""
assert old_volumes in s
s = s.replace(old_volumes, new_volumes, 1)

old_pg = """    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./docker/postgres/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro"""
new_pg = """    volumes:
      # Named volume, never a host bind mount: database data must never
      # land at a path inside this repository (see the `volumes:` block
      # above). ./docker/postgres/init is read-only committed SQL, and
      # the official image runs it ONLY on a genuinely first init (empty
      # data directory) — so changing POSTGRES_DB/PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME
      # against an existing volume does not create the new database.
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./docker/postgres/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro"""
assert old_pg in s
s = s.replace(old_pg, new_pg, 1)

old_storage = """    volumes:
      - storage-data:/data
      - ./docker/storage/s3-identities.json:/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json:ro"""
new_storage = """    volumes:
      # Named volume, never a host bind mount — same reason as postgres
      # above. The identities file is read-only committed development
      # configuration, not data.
      - storage-data:/data
      - ./docker/storage/s3-identities.json:/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json:ro"""
assert old_storage in s
s = s.replace(old_storage, new_storage, 1)

io.open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n").write(s)
print("ok")

## Persistence, lifecycle, and reset

Implements local sub-issue [02.03 — Configure local persistent volumes
and exclude them from version
control](../../../context/notion-tasks/sub-issues/02-03.md). Everything
below describes **local, disposable development data only** — there is no
production target, no external volume, and no backup or restore
mechanism anywhere in this stack.

### What persists, and where

Two Docker **named volumes** hold every byte of persistent state. One
PostgreSQL server with one physical volume holds *both* logical
databases — deliberately: a container or volume per database is not a
requirement of this stack and is not implemented.

| Owning service | Container path | Backed by | Holds | Disposable? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `postgres` | `/var/lib/postgresql/data` | named volume `<project>_postgres-data` | The whole PostgreSQL cluster: **both** logical databases (the Control DB `relis_control` *and* the project-test database `relis_project_example`), plus server-wide state (roles, WAL, the `postgres`/`template*` databases). | Yes |
| `storage` | `/data` | named volume `<project>_storage-data` | SeaweedFS's entire single-node state in one directory: master metadata, volume (object) files, and filer metadata — i.e. every bucket and non-production object. | Yes |

`<project>` is the Compose project name (see "Project scoping" below).
With the default startup from this directory that is `relis`, so the two
real volume names are `relis_postgres-data` and `relis_storage-data`.

Everything else mounted into a container is **configuration or source,
never generated data**:

| Owning service | Container path | Backed by | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `postgres` | `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` | `./docker/postgres/init` (read-only) | Committed first-init SQL. |
| `storage` | `/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json` | `./docker/storage/s3-identities.json` (read-only) | Committed development-only S3 identity. |
| `nginx` | `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` | `./docker/nginx/nginx.conf` (read-only) | Committed proxy routing. |
| `api` | `/app/apps/api/src` | `./apps/api/src` | Committed source, mounted for live reload. |
| `web` | `/app/apps/web/src`, `/app/apps/web/public` | `./apps/web/src`, `./apps/web/public` | Committed source/assets, mounted for live reload. |
| `worker` | `/app/apps/worker/src` | `./apps/worker/src` | Committed source, mounted for live reload. |
| `api`, `web`, `worker` | `/app/packages/config/src` | `./packages/config/src` | Committed shared-config source (see "Development mounts"). |

Generated **application** artifacts — `node_modules`, `dist`, `.next` —
are never mounted at all: each lives only inside its image/container
layer (see "Development mounts" above) and is rebuilt from the committed
lockfile and source. They are therefore not persistent across container
recreation either, and recreating a container re-derives them.

The consequence worth stating explicitly: **no service bind-mounts a
writable data directory out of this repository.** Database and object
data cannot become a tracked repository artifact, because no path in the
working tree ever holds any. `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts`
asserts this directly against the resolved Compose configuration, which
is a stronger guarantee than an ignore rule.

`.gitignore` covers the remaining cases: real environment files
(`.env`, `.env.*`, with `.env.example` the committed exception),
generated build output (`dist`, `.next`, `node_modules`), coverage, test
run output (`test-results/`, `playwright-report/`, `blob-report/`), and —
defensively — the generated-artifact directories the required structure
reserves at `storage/uploads/`, `storage/exports/`, and `storage/temp/`
(those do not exist yet and no application adapter writes to them).
`tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence-ignore-rules.test.ts`
verifies all of it with read-only Git commands, and additionally asserts
that no ignore pattern is broad enough to shadow a tracked source file.

### Project scoping

content.content:
### Docker Compose (local stack)

```bash
cp .env.example .env   # once, if not already done
docker compose up --build
```

Starts all seven required local-development responsibilities as real
processes/containers: `web`, `api`, `worker` (dev/watch mode, not a job
processor), `postgres` (Control DB + a disposable project-test database),
`nginx` (the only published entry point), `storage` (SeaweedFS's
S3-compatible endpoint), and `mailhog` (mail capture). Open
`http://localhost:8080/` for the app; `/api/health` and `/api/ready` are
reachable through the same proxy.

#### Lifecycle and reset

Local data lives in two Docker named volumes, `relis_postgres-data` (the
PostgreSQL server holding **both** the Control DB and the project-test
database) and `relis_storage-data` (every SeaweedFS bucket and object).
Data survives everything except an explicit reset:

```bash
docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml stop                              # stop, keep containers and data
docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml start                             # start again, same containers
docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans             # remove containers/network, KEEP data
docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml up -d                             # recreate containers, data intact
docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans   # RESET: permanently delete this project's data
```

⚠️ The last command is **irreversible** and destroys both local
databases and every stored object at once (they share one volume each).
There is no backup or restore. It never runs as part of ordinary
startup, and no broad `docker ... prune` is ever needed or
recommended — those reach beyond this project. Recreating afterward is
just `up -d --build`, which reprovisions both (empty) databases from
committed configuration.

Full service graph, address types (internal/host-facing/browser-public),
database isolation, the complete persistence inventory and lifecycle
table, exactly what a reset deletes, how to recreate the stack
afterward, and — importantly — this stack's **known limitations** (no
queue consumer, no storage/mail application adapter, empty schemas, no
seeds or backups) are documented in
[docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md](docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md).
Read that before relying on this stack for anything beyond local
iteration.

`pnpm run test:integration` exercises the stack with real, disposable
Compose projects (`tests/integration/docker-compose/`) — including the
persistence/reset/recreation lifecycle above and read-only Git checks
that stack data and environment files stay untracked; `pnpm run
test:e2e` additionally verifies the frontend's own browser-issued health
request through the proxy with a real Chromium instance
(`tests/e2e/docker-compose/`, via Playwright — requires its browser
binary installed with `pnpm exec playwright install chromium`, not run
automatically). Both require Docker; see
[docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md](docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md)
for exactly what each does and does not prove.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.content:
### Lifecycle operations

Always pass the project and file explicitly — `-p <project> -f
docker-compose.yml` — so a command can never act on a different project
than intended. (`docker compose` infers the project from the current
directory's name when `-p` is omitted; being explicit costs nothing and
removes the ambiguity entirely, which matters most for the last row.)

| Goal | Command | Containers | Named volumes | Data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Stop**, keeping containers and data | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml stop` | Stopped, **kept** | Kept | **Kept** |
| **Start** again (same containers) | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml start` | Restarted in place | Kept | **Kept** |
| **Restart** in one step | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml restart` | Restarted in place | Kept | **Kept** |
| **Remove containers and the network**, keeping data | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans` | **Removed** | **Kept** | **Kept** |
| Recreate after that removal | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml up -d` | Newly created | Reattached | **Kept** |
| **Reset** — delete this project's disposable data | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans` | **Removed** | **DELETED** | **DESTROYED** |

The only difference between the fourth row and the last is the
`--volumes` flag. That flag is the entire reset.

### ⚠️ Reset destroys data — read before running it

`docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans`
**permanently and irreversibly deletes**:

- `relis_postgres-data` — and with it **both** logical databases at
  once: the Control DB (`relis_control`) *and* the project-test database
  (`relis_project_example`), plus every table, row, and role on that
  server. They share one volume; there is no way to reset one and keep
  the other.
- `relis_storage-data` — and with it **every bucket and object** in the
  local SeaweedFS instance.

It does **not** touch: your source code, `.env`, any other Compose
project's containers or volumes, or the built images (those are a build
cache, removed separately and deliberately if ever wanted). There is no
backup, no snapshot, and no undo — this stack intentionally implements
none, because its data is local and disposable by design.

Substitute the real project name for `relis` if you started the stack
with a different `-p`. If you are unsure what a reset would delete, list
it first — a read-only check:

```bash
docker volume ls --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=relis
```

Never reset as part of ordinary startup: `up`, `up --build`, `stop`,
`start`, `restart`, and `down` (without `--volumes`) all keep data, and
that is the normal path.

**Do not** use broad commands to clean up instead. `docker system prune`,
`docker volume prune`, `docker builder prune --all`, a bare
`docker volume rm` against a guessed name, or deleting a directory with
`rm -rf` all reach beyond this project and can destroy unrelated
containers, volumes, and other developers' or other projects' data. The
scoped `down --volumes` above is the only reset this stack needs, which
is why **no reset script is provided**: the existing Compose commands and
this table are sufficient, and a script would add a second, more
dangerous way to do the same thing.

### Clean recreation after a reset

content.text:
Everything is clean and verified. Here's the final report.

## Sub-issue #48 — complete

### What already existed (reused, not rebuilt)
Sub-issue #47's stack already had two named volumes (`postgres-data`, `storage-data`), no bind-mounted data directory, and a `--volumes` flag on `down`. That groundwork was correct — #48 added the missing **verification**, **documentation**, and a couple of **missing helpers**, not a new architecture.

### Files changed (all inside `relis/`)
| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md` | New "Persistence, lifecycle, and reset" section: inventory table, project-scoping proof, full lifecycle table, explicit reset warning (what it destroys, what it doesn't), clean-recreation steps with honest empty-schema/no-seed/no-backup limitations. Updated Tests section and traceability header. |
| `README.md` | New "Lifecycle and reset" subsection with the stop/start/remove/reset commands and the irreversibility warning. |
| `docker-compose.yml` | Comments only (no behavior change): documents what each volume holds, why no `external`/fixed `name`, and the stop/remove/reset distinction. |
| `.env.example` | Comment noting first-init-only database creation and pointing at the lifecycle doc. |
| `.gitignore` | Added narrow, `.gitkeep`-preserving rules for `storage/{uploads,exports,temp}/` (the only real gap found — DB/object data was already structurally impossible to track, since nothing bind-mounts it). |
| `packages/test-utils/src/docker-compose.ts` | Added `composeStart`, `composeDownKeepVolumes`, `listContainerIds`, `listAllVolumeNames`, `listVolumeNamesByComposeProject`, `inspectVolume`/`volumeExists`, `resolveComposePersistence` (credential-free volume/bind-mount/DB-target inventory from `docker compose config --format json`). |
| `packages/test-utils/src/git.ts` (new) | Read-only Git helpers: `listTrackedFiles`, `listTrackedFilesMatchingIgnoreRules`, `listIgnoredPaths`, `listWorkingTreeEntries`. Nothing stages/commits anything. |
| `packages/test-utils/src/s3-sigv4.ts` | Corrected a stale "not yet verified" comment (it has been, repeatedly, since #47). |
| `tests/fixtures/docker-compose/persistence-fixtures.ts` (new) | Synthetic, non-sensitive DB/object fixtures (control, project, bystander). |
| `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts` (new) | Real-Docker persistence/reset/recreation suite (below). |
| `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence-ignore-rules.test.ts` (new) | Read-only Git ignore-rule suite (below). |

### Acceptance criteria → test evidence
| AC | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Control/project DBs logically separate, documented targets match Compose | `persistence.test.ts`: resolved `migrate-control`/`migrate-project` targets == `postgres:5432/relis_control` and `.../relis_project_persistence_test`; fixture row isolation asserted both directions |
| Fixture row + object survive stop/start | `persistence.test.ts` "retains... across a normal stop/start" — same container IDs confirmed |
| Survive container removal/recreation (volumes retained) | `persistence.test.ts` "retains... after container removal and recreation" — `down --remove-orphans` (no `--volumes`), new container IDs, volumes unchanged |
| Scoped reset removes only the disposable project's volumes | `persistence.test.ts` "removes ONLY this disposable project's volumes" — a **second independent Compose project** (`relis-bystander-*`) with its own volume/row proven untouched after the first's reset |
| Fresh stack recreates post-reset, prior fixtures absent | `persistence.test.ts` "recreates a fresh stack... with the prior fixtures absent" |
| Env secrets/generated data never tracked | `persistence-ignore-rules.test.ts` — `.env*`, generated output, `storage/{uploads,exports,temp}/` all ignored; `.env.example`/fixtures/config stay trackable; no tracked file is shadowed by an over-broad pattern (`git ls-files -i -c`) |
| Reset docs warn about data loss | `docker-compose-stack.md` "⚠️ Reset destroys data" section |

### Commands run (all from `relis/`)
- `npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts` → **10 passed, 1 skipped**, exit 0 (real Docker, ~132s)
- `npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence-ignore-rules.test.ts` → **6 passed, 1 skipped**, exit 0
- `pnpm run typecheck` → exit 0
- `pnpm run build` → exit 0 (web/api/worker)
- `pnpm -r test` → exit 0, **0 tests discovered** in any package (pre-existing `--passWithNoTests`; real coverage lives under root `tests/`)
- `pnpm run test:integration` (full suite, all 20 files) → **237 passed, 6 skipped, 0 failed**, exit 0
- `pnpm run lint` → **exit 1**, pre-existing and unrelated: `apps/web/src/app/page.tsx:47` `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` (file untouched by this change, last modified in commit `a3ab84a`)
- Docker state verified clean before/after: 0→0 volumes, 0→0 containers, no stray networks

### Test/volume identifiers used (all synthetic, disposable)
- Projects: `relis-persist-<random>`, `relis-bystander-<random>`
- Volumes destroyed by the in-test reset: `relis-persist-<random>_postgres-data`, `relis-persist-<random>_storage-data`
- Fixtures: `persistence_fixture_control`/`_project`/`_bystander` tables; S3 object `relis-persistence-fixture/persistence-fixture.txt`

### Safety
Ownership was confirmed via `com.docker.compose.project` labels immediately before the only destructive call; a pre-run baseline of all daemon volumes was diffed afterward (0 pre-existing volumes were destroyed); deletion was exclusively `docker compose -p <test-project> down --volumes` — no prune, no `docker volume rm`, no filesystem deletion. Cleanup ran in `afterAll` for both test projects independently and verified its own result.

### Remaining blockers / notes

1. Ownership checks must protect every destructive path.
In persistence.test.ts, afterAll currently calls cleanupComposeProject with --volumes even when ownership verification failed.
- Validate resolved volume names, project scoping, external flags, and the pre-existing-volume baseline BEFORE starting either test project.
- Verify ownership again before every destructive reset or cleanup, for both the main and bystander projects.
- If ownership cannot be established, refuse deletion and report the resources requiring manual inspection.
- Handle partial setup safely: clean up only resources confirmed to belong to this run, preserve the original failure, and report cleanup failures separately.

2. Distinguish absent volumes from Docker failures.
inspectVolume currently returns undefined for every nonzero exit.
- Return absence only when the volume is genuinely not found.
- Throw on daemon, permission, command, or malformed-output errors.
- Ensure volumeExists cannot turn an inspection failure into a successful deletion assertion.

3. Prove actual object absence after reset.
Replace the status >= 400 assertion in persistence.test.ts with a specific S3 missing-resource response: HTTP 404 and NoSuchBucket or NoSuchKey, as applicable.
Do not accept authentication failures, server errors, or connection failures as evidence of deletion. Confirm the storage service is operational after recreation.

Add regression coverage for ownership rejection, partial setup, inspection errors versus genuine absence, and rejection of unrelated S3 errors. Test unsafe scenarios with controlled fakes or disposable fixtures—never endanger existing user volumes.

Run focused tests, relevant typechecks, and the real disposable persistence/reset/recreation suite. Verify final cleanup. Do not weaken assertions, use broad prune commands, restart Docker without approval, or touch unrelated resources.

Do not browse, change application behavior, commit, push, or advance to another sub-issue. Report changes, exact verification results, and any remaining blockers before declaring #48 complete.

content.content:
"use strict";

/**
 * Preloaded via `node --require <this file>` into a REAL entry point
 * (apps/web/scripts/run.mjs, tooling/scripts/deploy.mjs,
 * packages/database/src/migrate.ts, ...) so a test can observe exactly
 * what that entry point decided to spawn — the command, its arguments,
 * working directory, and the relevant forwarded environment variables —
 * without ever launching the real target process (Next.js, Prisma, a
 * built service, ...) or opening a listener.
 *
 * Patches the shared node:child_process module BEFORE the target's own
 * `import { spawn } from "node:child_process"` executes. Node's ESM named
 * imports of core modules are live bindings onto the underlying
 * CommonJS exports object, so this CommonJS-side reassignment (done here,
 * before the target's module graph loads) is what its later call sees.
 *
 * The captured invocation is printed as one line prefixed with
 * "SPAWN_CAPTURED:" followed by JSON, then the process exits immediately
 * — nothing resembling a real child process is ever created. Only the
 * first spawn() call is captured (the process exits before a second could
 * occur); this fixture is for asserting what the FIRST attempted spawn
 * would be, not a full call log.
 */
const childProcess = require("node:child_process");

// Curated rather than the entire process.env: broad enough to cover every
// entry point that currently uses this fixture, without dumping unrelated
// noise into the captured JSON. Values here are always synthetic test
// fixtures, never real secrets.
const CAPTURED_ENV_KEYS = [
  "NODE_ENV",
  "WEB_PORT",
  "NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL",
  "API_PORT",
  "API_HOST",
  "API_CORS_ORIGIN",
  "CONTROL_DATABASE_URL",
  "PROJECT_DATABASE_URL",
];

Clean — only the intended files from this session plus the carried-over sub-issue #48 work. All changes stayed inside `relis/`.

## Summary: Fixes to the 3 review findings

### 1. Ownership checks must protect every destructive path
- **`packages/test-utils/src/docker-compose.ts`**: added `checkVolumeOwnershipForDeletion` (pure), `checkProvisioningSafety`/`assertProvisioningSafety` (pure, validates volume naming/`external`/baseline *before* provisioning), `verifyVolumeOwnershipForDeletion`/`verifyAllVolumesOwnedForDeletion` (real-Docker gate), and `cleanupDisposableTargets`/`listOwnedVolumesWithOwnership` (multi-target orchestrator: per-target try/catch, ownership re-verified immediately before every destructive call, refuses `--volumes` and reports exactly which volumes "require manual inspection" when ownership can't be established, keeps processing other targets, never confuses one target's failure for another's).
- **`tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts`**: `beforeAll` now calls `assertProvisioningSafety` for both projects *before* any container starts. `afterAll` now uses `cleanupDisposableTargets` for **both** the primary and bystander projects (previously the bystander was destroyed with zero ownership check — the core bug). The mid-suite reset test re-verifies ownership via `verifyAllVolumesOwnedForDeletion` immediately before its own destructive call.

### 2. Distinguish absent volumes from Docker failures
- `inspectVolume` now classifies failures via `isVolumeNotFoundError` (matches Docker's literal "no such volume" response only) — returns `undefined` only for genuine absence, **throws** on daemon-unreachable, permission, or malformed-JSON-on-exit-0 failures. `volumeExists` inherits this (a failed check can no longer read as "deleted").

### 3. Prove actual object absence after reset
- **`packages/test-utils/src/s3-sigv4.ts`**: added `parseS3ErrorBody`, `readS3ErrorResponse`, `isS3ObjectAbsent` — absence requires HTTP 404 **and** `Code` of `NoSuchKey`/`NoSuchBucket`; auth failures, 5xx, and unparseable bodies are explicitly rejected.
- **`persistence.test.ts`**: the final test now does a real liveness put/get against a fresh bucket (proving storage is operational) *before* asserting the old fixture is specifically `404 NoSuchKey`/`NoSuchBucket`.

### New regression coverage — `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence-safety.test.ts` (33 tests, no real Docker required except one safe read-only inspect)
Ownership rejection (mismatched project, pre-existing/baseline, `external:true`, undefined ownership), provisioning-safety rejection, `cleanupDisposableTargets` partial-setup/independent-target-processing with fakes, `isVolumeNotFoundError` classification, and S3 error classification (NoSuchKey/NoSuchBucket accepted; AccessDenied/5xx/malformed rejected).

message.content:
Fix the remaining cleanup-safety gap in sub-issue #48.

Currently, afterAll checks only volumes returned by listOwnedVolumesWithOwnership (filtered by the Compose project label), then calls docker compose down --volumes. A configured volume with an incorrect or missing label can therefore escape inspection while still being targeted by the destructive command.

Requirements:
- Before every destructive cleanup, inspect the union of volume names resolved from the exact Compose configuration used for cleanup and volumes discovered through project labels.
- Block volume deletion if any existing target is pre-existing, external, incorrectly labeled, or cannot be inspected. If configuration resolution fails, fail closed.
- Treat confirmed absence separately from inspection failure: a genuinely absent volume does not require deletion; a failed inspection must block it.
- Preserve independent cleanup of primary and bystander projects and clear reporting of resources requiring manual inspection.
- Add a regression test with two configured volumes: one correctly labeled and another with an incorrect or missing project label that is absent from label-based discovery. Assert that destructive cleanup is never called.

Follow the existing stack, project structure, and testing policy. Keep changes scoped to this safety fix; do not start another sub-issue.

Run the relevant regression tests and typechecks. Run real persistence verification only with uniquely named disposable resources and the corrected guards. Do not prune, restart Docker, or touch existing user resources. Report actual results and limitations. Do not commit or push.

content.text:
Clean — only the intended files from this session plus the carried-over #48 work. All changes stayed inside `relis/`.

## Summary: Cleanup-safety gap fixed

### The gap
`afterAll` only inspected volumes `listOwnedVolumesWithOwnership` discovered **via the Compose project label filter**, then called `docker compose down --volumes`. But `down --volumes` targets volumes by **name** (from the resolved Compose config), not by label — so a volume with the right name but an incorrect/missing `com.docker.compose.project` label would never be inspected, yet would still be destroyed.

### Fix — `packages/test-utils/src/docker-compose.ts`
- **`VolumeInspectionResult`** (tri-state: `"exists"` / `"absent"` / `"failed"`) + **`OwnedVolumeRecord`** — absence and inspection-failure are now distinct types, not conflated.
- **`checkVolumeOwnershipForDeletion`** (rewritten, pure): `"absent"` → always `ok:true` (nothing to delete, never a blocker); `"failed"` → always `ok:false` (must block); `"exists"` → the existing baseline/label/external checks.
- **`evaluateOwnershipGate`** (new, pure/sync) replaces the old async `verifyAllVolumesOwnedForDeletion`.
- **`VolumeDiscoverySources` + `discoverVolumesRequiringInspection`** (new): builds the **union** of `resolveConfiguredVolumeNames()` (fresh, from the exact Compose config) and `listLabeledVolumeNames()`, inspects every name in that union. **Fails closed** — rejects entirely if either source rejects. A single name's inspection failure doesn't abort the others' discovery (full visibility), but still blocks the batch via the gate.
- **`createComposeCleanupTarget`** (new): the real-Docker wiring — re-resolves Compose config fresh at cleanup time (fail-closed on resolution failure), builds the union, inspects, and constructs a fully-wired `DisposableCleanupTarget`.
- **`cleanupDisposableTargets`**: now calls `discoverVolumes()` → `evaluateOwnershipGate()`; only volumes confirmed `"exists"` are reported `volumesDeleted`.
- Removed the superseded `listOwnedVolumesWithOwnership`, `verifyVolumeOwnershipForDeletion`, `verifyAllVolumesOwnedForDeletion`.

### `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts`
- `afterAll` now builds both targets via `createComposeCleanupTarget` (union discovery, fail-closed, fresh resolution) for **both** primary and bystander projects independently.
- The mid-suite scoped-reset test now also re-resolves fresh and runs the same union-based gate before its own destructive call.

content.text:
Clean — only intended files. All changes stayed inside `relis/`.

## Summary: Environment-consistency gap fixed

### The gap
`createComposeCleanupTarget` passed `env` to `resolveComposePersistence` (config resolution) but **not** to `removeContainersKeepingVolumesOrThrow`/`cleanupComposeProject` (the actual cleanup commands) — those called `composeDownKeepVolumes`/`composeDown` with no `env` option at all, silently falling back to the test process's own inherited environment. If any resolved config value (a volume name, port, or database target) depended on an env var, the gate could validate against one configuration while the destructive command targeted a different one.

### Fix
**`packages/test-utils/src/docker-compose.ts`**
- `composeDown`, `cleanupComposeProject`, `composeDownKeepVolumes`, `removeContainersKeepingVolumesOrThrow` now all accept `options.env?: ComposeEnv`, merged via the same `withEnv()` helper `composeUp`/`composeConfigQuiet` already use. **Optional, defaulting to `{}`** — every existing caller (`stack-smoke.test.ts`, `config-validation.test.ts`, `dependency-unavailable.test.ts`, `web-health-check.spec.ts`) compiles and behaves identically, untouched.
- `createComposeCleanupTarget` now threads its own `env` parameter into **both** `removeContainersKeepingVolumes` and `removeContainersAndVolumes`, so the exact overrides used to resolve configuration are the exact overrides used to tear it down.

**`tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts`**
- Mid-suite scoped-reset test's destructive `cleanupComposeProject` call now passes `env: composeEnv` (same env used by the fresh `resolveComposePersistence` call just above it).
- Updated header comment documenting the guarantee for both primary and bystander cleanup.

### New regression coverage — `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence-cleanup-env.test.ts` (new file, 3 tests)
Mocks `runToCompletion` (the single choke point every Compose/`docker` call in `docker-compose.ts` goes through) via `vi.mock` + `vi.importActual`, with a fake `docker compose config --format json` response whose **volume names are derived directly from an env var** (`TEST_VOLUME_SUFFIX`). Proves:
1. The destructive path (`down --volumes`) receives the identical env, including the volume-naming variable.
2. The volume-preserving path (`down --remove-orphans`, when the gate blocks) receives it too.
3. Two concurrently-processed targets (primary/bystander) never cross-contaminate each other's env.

Kept in its **own file** (not added to `persistence-safety.test.ts`) because `vi.mock` applies file-wide — mixing it into the file with the existing real-Docker `inspectVolume` check would have silently broken that check by routing it through the mock too. Confirmed via a manual sanity check: temporarily reverting the fix made all 3 new tests fail with the exact expected `undefined` mismatch; restoring the fix made them pass again.

### Verification
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `pnpm --filter @relis/test-utils typecheck` | exit 0 |
| `pnpm run typecheck` (full workspace) | exit 0 |
| `pnpm run build` | exit 0 |
| `persistence-cleanup-env.test.ts` (mocked) | **3 passed**, exit 0 |
| Same + `persistence-safety.test.ts` + `persistence-ignore-rules.test.ts` together | **52 passed, 1 skipped**, exit 0 (confirms no mock leakage) |
| `persistence.test.ts` (real Docker, destructive, project `relis-persist-b18586d8` + bystander) | **10 passed**, 1 skipped, exit 0, 137s |
| `pnpm run test:integration` (all 22 files) | **283 passed**, 6 skipped, 0 failed, exit 0 |
| `pnpm run lint` | exit 1 — pre-existing, unrelated (`apps/web/src/app/page.tsx`, untouched) |
| Docker state before/after real suite | 0→0 volumes, 0→0 containers, 0→0 networks |
| Sanity check: regression test fails without fix | Confirmed (3/3 fail with exact expected diff), passes with fix restored |

Next.js's build again auto-reformatted `apps/web/tsconfig.json`; reverted, not part of this change.

No commits, no pushes, no Docker prune/restart, no other sub-issue started.
